checked.label: hope-free-now 65 in 100
problems: Checked in PMC3227547 (NCBI full text, fetched 2026-11-05): Table 1 'Cannabis Dependence (N=530) % (95%CI)', Tables 3 and 4 'Cannabis remission (N=344)'; 344/530 = 64.9%, so '65 in 100' and '344 of 530' are the source's head counts. Remission is 'finally stopped having any of these experiences (dependence criteria) ... they never started happening again', which backs 'free of every sign of it'. DSM-IV dependence is '3 or more of the 7 ... criteria within a 12 month period'. The limits section names 'overreport of remission' and institutionalized people not sampled. Quote is two table cells, word for word, 7 words.
Note, not blocking (same as the last round): 'Weed was weaker in 2001 than today' is not in this source. It is true elsewhere.

checked.label: hope-lifetime 97%
problems: Checked: '97.2% for cannabis' lifetime, '66.2% for cannabis' a decade after onset. The ethnic-group sentence in alsoRef is word for word, 28 words; 81.6% to 95.6% rounds to 82% to 96%. 'Projected' is in the headline (rule 10). The limits say not sampling institutionalized people leads 'to overestimation of the cumulative probability of remission', which backs 'probably lower'. Men: 'Men were less likely than women to remit from dependence on all the substances assessed'. Main quote word for word with an ellipsis.

checked.label: who-years 6 years
problems: Checked: 'Half of the cases of nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine dependence remitted approximately 26, 14, 6 and 5 years after dependence onset'. The quote's ellipses only drop the other drugs (rule 13). The new mirror ('takes decades') is answered by the figure. The new caveat sentence matches the same paper's 97.2% lifetime projection. Headline says 'projected'.
Note, not blocking: the 2001 potency line is not from this source (see item 0).

checked.label: who-age Age 29
problems: basis.measured 'their addiction lasted about 12 years' misreads the 11.74. The paper's Methods define it: 'We used these data to calculate “addiction career” duration, the number of years from age of first use for any substance to the age at which they resolved their alcohol or other drug problem.' So the 12 years run from first use, not from when the addiction began. The time hooked was shorter than that.

The reviser dropped the last round's wording because 15.26 to 28.87 is 13.6 years. That gap is inside the paper: an average of each person's span need not equal the difference of two group averages. The paper still defines the 11.74 from first use. The fix keeps the 12 and says what it counts, as the paper's own figure.

Rest checked in PMC5992615: quote word for word, 20 words (M = 28.87; 99% CI 26.46, 31.29). First use 15.26, weekly use 16.89 (Table 1b). Header 'Cannabis (12.6%, n = 217)', note 'Displaying weighted counts'. History of alcohol problems 48.44% and of other drug problems 33.34% back 'Many also had a past problem with another substance'. 'About 1 in 6 diagnosed' comes from the sister paper on the same survey (Kelly 2017 Table 1: alcohol/substance use disorder diagnosis 17.0%). The new mirror is fine.

fix.basis.measured: Age when the problem ended, as people remembered it. On average they first used weed at 15 and weekly at about 17. The paper puts the time from first use to the end of the problem at about 12 years.

checked.label: how-alone 54 in 100
problems: Checked in PMC6076174: Table 3 row 'Cannabis (e.g., marijuana, hashish) | 45.8 | 5.53 |' (assisted %, SE), so 100 - 45.8 = 54.2 used no help. 1.96 x 5.53 = 10.8 points gives about 43% to 65% unassisted (plain arithmetic on the source's SE). 'Assisted' = lifetime use of outpatient or inpatient treatment, 'anti-relapse/craving medication', mutual-help groups or community recovery support 'e.g., sober living environments'. Table 1: cannabis 11.0% of 2,002, about 220. Greater severity went with assisted pathways. Quote is the table row word for word. The headline is not more hopeful than the source.

checked.label: how-tries 2 tries
problems: Checked in PMC6602820 Table 1: 'Cannabis | 4.62 (8.41) | 2 (1, 4) | 0, 100'. The median of 2 backs 'half needed 2 or fewer'. The IQR (1, 4) backs the quarters. A minimum of 0 means zero-try answers are counted. The Discussion says some 'did not count the current attempt'. Mean 4.62 is 'about 5'. Quote is table cells word for word.
Note, not blocking: this paper gives no cannabis n. 'About 217' comes from the sister paper on the same survey (Kelly 2018, weighted n = 217).

checked.label: how-abrupt 85%
problems: counted 'daily weed users, not checked for addiction' is literally false. All were checked: the DSM Checklist for Cannabis Use Disorder was one of the baseline scales, and 'Most (75%) met criteria for DSM- 5 Cannabis Use Disorder using a self-report version of the DSM checklist'. What the paper leaves out is how severe it was: it reports any disorder, mild included, and gives no moderate-to-severe count. So the honest label is that the number who were hooked is not reported. This matches the wording on the memory-trial card ('addiction not reported'), which has the same situation. It keeps the 'not' the build needs on a heavy chip.

Rest checked in PMC4877269: quote word for word ('Most (85%) participants made an intentional reduction attempt during the study.'), 46% quit attempt, 'At 6 month follow-up, 8% of participants had not used cannabis in the last month', 'at least 5 days/week', 193 people, recruited 1/2010 to 3/2012, mean age 32, 53% men, paid $2 a day. 'almost all attempts to stop or reduce cannabis lasted less than a week'. 'Ten participants sought treatment during the study (6% of those who intentionally tried ...)'. 'abstinence and reduction predicted decreases in cannabis dependence'. The new mirror is 14 words.

Note, not blocking: 'not in treatment' in basis.who is not an entry rule in the paper. The paper calls them users 'trying to change on their own', and 10 sought treatment during the study (the caveat says so).

fix.counted: daily weed users; how many were hooked is not reported

checked.label: helps-medicine 27 vs 26 in 100
problems: Checked in PMC12481667 (PMC page, Summary of findings 1): 'Participants abstinent at end of treatment | 262 per 1000 | 270 per 1000 (184 to 396) | RR 1.03 (0.70 to 1.51) | 290 (4 RCTs) | Moderate'. 27 vs 26 in 100 are the review's own arm figures, rounded. SoF 4 (NAC): 352 vs 411 per 1000, 270 (2 RCTs), Moderate, so 35 vs 41 in 100. SoF 2 (CBD): 68 (1 RCT), Low. SoF 3 (anticonvulsants and mood stabilisers): 29 (1 RCT), Very low.

The new headline lead is backed: 'There are currently no medicines specifically for the treatment of cannabis use disorder'. The plain-language summary also says 'For stopping cannabis use by the end of treatment, THC preparations, CBD, N-acetylcysteine, oxytocin and PF-04457845 are probably ineffective'. The new measured sentence is backed: 'Narrative data from individual studies suggest that THC, cannabidiol and PF-04457845 can reduce cannabis withdrawal symptoms, and THC can also reduce cravings.' Also checked: 37 RCTs with 3,201 people; USA 29, Australia 4, Israel 2, Canada 1, UK 1; 32 trials mostly male; searched May 2024. The quote is table cells word for word, 26 words. The headline is 22 words and carries one pair.

checked.label: helps-talk 23 vs 12 in 100
problems: caveat 'More than 4 sessions over more than a month did better than shorter therapy' leaves out the source's time limit. The review says high-intensity interventions 'produced consistently improved outcomes (particularly in terms of cannabis use frequency and severity of dependence) in the short term as compared with low-intensity interventions.' Without 'in the short term' the line is more hopeful than the source, and it sits right after 'No kind of therapy clearly worked at 9 months or later'.

Rest checked in PMC4914383 (PMC page): quote word for word, 25 words ('to 23% at follow-up of longer than four months. In contrast, an average of 12% of those in control conditions reported PPA at final follow-up.'). 'Across the eight studies reporting rates of PPA, an average of 37% ... at end of treatment'. PPA is 'abstinence for the month before assessment'. 'Half of the reviewed studies included collateral verification or urinalysis'. RR 2.55 (1.34 to 4.83), 6 studies, 1,166 people, low quality, at short-term follow-up. 'no particular intervention was consistently effective at nine-month follow-up or later'. 'data from five out of six studies supported the utility of adding voucher-based incentives ... on cannabis use frequency'. 'approximately one-quarter of participants abstinent at final follow-up'. Also: 23 trials, 4,045 people, about 7 sessions over about 12 weeks, before July 2015, 15 US trials. The SoF gives no per-100 arm pair ('an average of 23.02% across treatments'), so the averages stay. The new headline time label ('at the later check-ups') and the measured split by time match the source.

fix.caveat: Averages across trials, not one head count, and the last check-up came at different times. In the 6 trials that could be combined (1,166 people), more were off weed at about 4 months with therapy than without, but the review calls that evidence weak. No kind of therapy clearly worked at 9 months or later. In the short term, more than 4 sessions over more than a month did better than shorter therapy; adding rewards for clean urine tests cut smoking days further in 5 of 6 trials.

checked.label: how-withdrawal Day 2-6
problems: The caveat's new clause ('irritability and anger often peak later, past the first week') is true, but the card's ref (the Budney 2003 abstract) does not contain it. It comes from Hesse 2013 (PMC4015312, fetched 2026-11-05). Its Table 5 gives the irritability/anger peak as day 14, and day 8.33 from Budney's own data. Its discussion says so in words. The fix adds that source as alsoRef so a later checker can find the line; no reader text changes.

Rest checked against the PubMed abstract (PMID 12943018; the full text is paywalled, Unpaywall shows no open copy): 18 users, 5 days of usual use then 45 days off, 12 ex-users, the listed symptoms. The quote is word for word, 17 words. The new mirror is backed: restlessness and sleep problems are in the list, and they peaked early (Hesse Table 5 from Budney: restlessness day 4, insomnia day 2).
Open doubt from the last round, still open: the abstract does not say whether the 18 were checked for dependence. 'Vermont, USA' comes from the authors' address.

alsoRef.cite: Hesse M, Thylstrup B (2013). Time-course of the DSM-5 cannabis withdrawal symptoms in poly-substance abusers. BMC Psychiatry 13:258.
alsoRef.quote: In the later phase of withdrawal came irritability/anger, and vivid, unpleasant dreams, with peaks later than a week after cessation.

checked.label: how-withdrawal 47%
problems: Checked against the PubMed abstract and PMC7146100 full text: 'The overall pooled prevalence of CWS was 47% (6469 of 23 518) (95% CI, 41%-52%)'. The quote is word for word, 20 words. 47 studies, 23,518 people, 69% men, median age 29.9, searched to June 19, 2019. Population 17%, outpatient 54%, inpatient 87%. Daily use was linked to a higher rate. Studies came from the USA, Germany, France, Brazil, Canada, Australia and others ('several countries'). 6,469/23,518 = 27.5%, so 'about 28 in 100' is plain arithmetic. The new headline drops the '47 studies' clash and adds no figure.
Note, not blocking: 'got withdrawal symptoms' is looser than 'met the criteria for withdrawal' in measured. That makes the headline more cautious, not less.

checked.label: how-slips 71%
problems: Checked against the PubMed abstract (PMID 14629990): '82 individuals who achieved at least 2 weeks of abstinence during outpatient treatment for marijuana dependence'. 'Seventy-one percent used marijuana at least once (i.e., lapsed) within 6 months of initial abstinence, averaging 73 days (SD = 50) till lapsing.' The quote is word for word, 23 words. The caveat's 'most' stands for the abstract's second 71% ('71% of those who lapsed, relapsed to heavier use defined as at least 4 days of marijuana use in any 7-day period'). 'Early lapses were more strongly associated with consequent relapse.' The headline is 21 words, with one figure plus its time window.

checked.label: after-first-month 72 hours
problems: Checked against the PubMed abstract (PMID 29710074): 'studies requiring an abstinence period longer than 72 hours (15 studies; n = 928) had an overall effect size (d, -0.08; 95% CI, -0.22 to 0.07) that was not significantly different from 0'. The quote is word for word with an ellipsis, 29 words. n = 928 is users plus comparison people: 928 + 7,799 = 8,727 = 2,152 users + 6,575 comparison people. Users' average age 20.6, 68.4% male; search through May 2017. The source's own conclusion ('abstinence of longer than 72 hours diminishes cognitive deficits') is at least as hopeful as the new headline. The headline is 22 words.

checked.label: after-first-month Week 1
problems: Checked in PMC6587572 and the PubMed abstract: aged 16-25, from the community and a high school, July 2015 to December 2016. MJ-Abst n = 62 (contingency management, urine-verified), MJ-Mon n = 26; '55 (88.7%) met a priori criteria for biochemically confirmed 30-day continuous abstinence'. Table 1: past-90-day use days 54.4 and 57.5 ('about 55 of the last 90'). A CUDIT-R was taken at baseline, with no diagnosis count reported. 'There was no effect of abstinence on attention: both groups improved similarly'. 'Future studies are needed to determine whether the improvement ... is associated with improvement in academic and other functional outcomes'. The quote is word for word with an ellipsis, 24 words. The new design wording ('a fair test, split by chance') is right: 'Participants were randomly assigned'.

checked.label: after-mood +12 points
problems: Checked in PMC5846101: abstinent people scored 'higher QLES-Q-SF raw score on average by 6.78 points (or 12% of the maximum possible change in QLES-Q-SF score) compared to those who continued to use cannabis'. Baseline 49.83 raw is 'equivalent to 64.0% of the maximum possible score'. On that same 0-100 scale the gap is 12 points, so '12 points higher, out of 100' and 'about 64 out of 100' use one scale. Model 1 has F(1,47) and Figure 1 has N = 52. 29/62 were abstinent in the last 2 weeks. All had DSM-IV dependence and 'all were daily users'. The trial was 11 weeks, lofexidine + dronabinol vs placebo. Fewer using days were linked to better life quality; grams were not (p = .62). The paper names reverse direction as possible ('improved QoL may precede reduction in cannabis use').

The main quote is word for word, 28 words. The new alsoRef quote is word for word, 17 words; it ends before 'for major depressive disorder', which keeps another condition off the page and changes no meaning. The new caveat line ('big enough to matter') matches 'This is a clinically meaningful improvement'.
